title: Speak Software
text: Preface

title: Speak Software
text:
Why This Book Exists
Somewhere in a shared drive right now is software that runs a real business, written by someone who cannot read a line of code. A booking page. An invoice checker. A dashboard the boss looks at every morning. It was built by describing what was wanted, in plain language, to an AI agent — and it works.
The software industry does not know what to do with this. Neither do the schools. The old answer was: learn to code, for years, then build. The new answer from the hype machine is: stop learning, just vibe. Both are wrong, and the gap between them is where this book lives.
Programming has moved up an abstraction level. That has happened before — machine code to assembly, assembly to languages, languages to frameworks — and every time, two things happened. More people could build. And the durable skills moved up with it: not the syntax, but the thinking underneath. Specification. Decomposition. Verification. Taste. This book teaches those skills at the newest layer: you describe, an agent builds, and you are the one who decides whether it is true.
We call the bad version of this vibe coding — prompting until something looks right, never asking why. This book is not against it. Vibe coding is a legitimate tool for prototypes with a small blast radius, and pretending otherwise is gatekeeping. What this book is against is unmanaged vibe coding: shipping a black box to real users, with real data, and no way to know when it breaks. Boris Cherny, who built Claude Code at Anthropic, put the industry’s best current answer simply: prototypes can be black boxes, but production code written by AI should be held to a higher standard than human code — and that standard is met with guardrails, not heroics. The developer’s role is no longer the builder. It is the mini CEO of a department of one.

title: Speak Software
text:
The Department of One
Here is the frame for the whole book. You have been handed an engineering department: brilliant, tireless, overconfident, and it forgets everything you do not write down. One agent is an intern. A folder of well-written instructions turns it into a specialist. A filing cabinet of those folders turns it into a department. Twelve laboratories — each a real client brief, each killing one misconception — teach you to run it.
The companion labs are free and live at michael-borck.github.io/programming-labs. This book is the narrative and the harness: the why behind each lab, the guardrails the labs leave you to build, and the management layer that turns twelve exercises into a working practice.

title: Speak Software
text:
Who This Book Is For

Business-minded people who will never write code by hand — and should not have to
Students and career changers who want to build real things now
Developers’ colleagues and managers who need to evaluate AI-built software
Programmers, too: the management layer here is the one your job is becoming

title: Speak Software
text:
What This Book Is Not
It is not a Python book. You will not learn syntax; you will learn to specify so precisely that syntax stops being the bottleneck. (Code Python, Consult AI is the book for the language itself.)
It is not a prompt cookbook. Prompts appear throughout, but a prompt without a specification, a verification plan, and a decision log is delegation with extra steps.
It is not an argument that AI always gets it right. A third of this book is about the opposite: AI output is a hypothesis, and the guarded pipeline — not your confidence — is the verdict.
And it is not Converse Python, Partner AI, its companion on the shelf. That book teaches you to programme alongside AI, line by considered line. This one assumes you will never touch the code at all — and teaches you to direct anyway. If you cannot decide between them: if you want a language under your fingers, choose the companion; if you want a department at your command, choose this.

title: Speak Software
text:
If You Are Feeling Uncertain
You do not need to be “technical”. That word is a gatekeeper, and the gate it guards just moved. If you can write a clear email, you can write a clear specification. If you can organise a folder, you can organise a department. The people who appear to have mastered AI tools are weeks ahead, not years. This book starts where you are.

title: Speak Software
text:
How This Book Is Structured
Part I: The Department of One — the frame, the slop question, and the first spec. Part II: The Guardrails — checklists that run, version control as a flight recorder, context that persists, evidence of done, and the assembled slop defence. Part III: Judgement — taste, the last 20%, the filing cabinet of skills, and slop in the supply chain. Part IV: The Mini CEO — decomposition, audits, shipping, and the staff of sub-agents you will one day manage.
Every chapter pairs a lab from the companion series with the reasoning the lab leaves implicit, and closes by building one piece of the harness you will rely on for everything after.

title: 1  Hello, Department of One
text:
You are not learning to code. You are learning to run the people who do — and there is only one of them.

Lab companion: Lab 1. This chapter installs the frame: your AI agent is a brilliant, tireless, overconfident intern, and everything it does for you must live in a repository. You will set up GitHub, meet your agent, and ship a first change to a real repository — establishing the habit that separates a builder of demos from the owner of a department: if it is not in the repo, it does not exist.

title: 2  The Slop Question
text:
The dispute is not restrained versus vibe. It is: what is the blast radius?

New chapter — the framing. Boris Cherny, creator of Claude Code, was asked “what to do about slop?” by a developer torn between auditing every line and treating AI output as a black box. His answer anchors this book: black-box treatment is fine for throw-away prototypes with a small blast radius; production code written by AI deserves a higher bar than human code, met with automated guardrails. This chapter defines the terms — slop, blast radius, black-box threshold, guardrail — and ends with the reader’s own first blast-radius judgement.

title: 3  The Demo Illusion
text:
“It works” is the beginning of the sentence, not the end.

Lab companion: Lab 2. The demo always works, because the demo is the path you practised. This chapter builds the habit of defining done before admiring anything: acceptance criteria written before the agent runs, tested after. Introduces the evidence trio — SPEC.md, DECISIONS.md, CRITIQUE.md — that every subsequent chapter and every graded artefact in the series revolves around.

title: 4  Say What You Mean
text:
The AI knows what you said. It does not know what you meant.

Lab companion: Lab 3 (standalone; doubles as the series taster). Specification-first development: write SPEC.md as if handing it to a stranger, because you are. Introduces the Replication Test — your spec, alone, handed to a fresh agent must reproduce a product you would accept. If it does, you have authored a program in English.

title: 5  The Checklist It Can’t Charm
text:
Re-reading is not checking. A checklist that cannot run is a wish.

Lab companion: Lab 4. Acceptance checks become executable: a list a script can verify, so charm cannot talk its way past done. You will commission your first check script from the agent — and learn what to ask for so the checks fail loudly rather than pass politely.
crumbs: 5  The Checklist It Can't Charm

title: 6  The Flight Recorder
text:
One wrong move ruins nothing, if everything is recorded.

Lab companion: Lab 5. Version control as the department’s flight recorder: small commits, fearless branches, revert as a first-class move. The agent drives git; you own the discipline — commit size, message honesty, branch naming — because the trail is the only thing an audit can read later.

title: 7  Teach the Intern
text:
Every chat that starts from zero wastes everything you already learned.

Lab companion: Lab 6. The context folder: AGENTS.md and the standing documents that make the agent arrive already briefed. This is the seed of the skill-folder architecture — one department, taught once, consulted on demand.

title: 8  Trust, Then Verify
text:
“It sounds right” is the most expensive sentence in AI-assisted work.

Lab companion: Lab 7. Demanding evidence of done: outputs shown, checks run, receipts attached. Introduces VET from Conversation, Not Delegation (Verify, Explain, Test) as the reader’s reflex, and treats the agent’s explanation as a hypothesis rather than a verdict.

title: 9  The Slop Defence
text:
You cannot read every line. You can refuse to ship without a gate.

New chapter — the harness. Assembles the guardrails Cherny names into one beginner-scale gate: lint rules, tests with a coverage floor, a TODO/FIXME sweep, a diff-size budget, and a CI recipe the reader commissions from the agent rather than hand-writes. The chapter’s product is a slop-defence kit the reader will attach to every repo for the rest of the book.

title: 10  The Taste Test
text:
“Best” is not objective. That is precisely why they need you.

Lab companion: Lab 8. Critique as a deliverable: the reader reviews two plausible implementations and writes CRITIQUE.md with arguable opinions — not verdicts, positions. Taste is presented as the durable human contribution the mini CEO cannot delegate.

title: 11  The Last 20%
text:
The first 80% is a demo. The last 20% is the product.

Lab companion: Lab 9. Directing polish: what to leave alone, what to demand, and how to specify refinement without specifying pixels. The agent generates; the reader decides which gaps matter.

title: 12  The Filing Cabinet
text:
The most sophisticated AI orchestration is a well-organised folder.

New chapter — the skill-folder architecture. The context wall, and why an agent with a filing cabinet beats seven bespoke frameworks: SKILL.md instructions plus scripts, read on demand by one capable agent, spawning specialists on the fly. Builds the reader’s first skill folder for a repeatable personal workflow, and connects Lab 6’s context folder to the company-scale pattern.

title: 13  Slop in the Supply Chain
text:
The agent does not just write code. It chooses what to trust.

New chapter — the sharpest real risk. Hallucinated packages (slopsquatting), dependency vetting, licence and attribution of AI-generated code, and the short list of what must never be pasted into any tool. The reader runs a dependency audit on their own lab product and writes a trust policy into their context folder.
crumbs: 13  Slop in the Supply Chain

title: 14  Run the Department
text:
Big things are not built in one go. They are decomposed, dispatched, and verified.

Lab companion: Lab 10. Managing work as issues: decomposition into briefs a fresh agent can execute, sequenced so each lands on verified ground. The mini CEO’s first management system.

title: 15  The Audit
text:
The code is not the only record. Sometimes it is not even the true one.

Lab companion: Lab 11. Reading someone else’s trail — a provided repo with its spec, decisions and critique — and judging whether the product matches its story. The marking model of the series, made student-facing.

title: 16  Ship Something True
text:
You do not need permission to ship. You need evidence it is true.

Lab companion: Lab 12. The full loop owned end to end: brief, spec, build, gate, ship, critique. The portfolio that is the evidence of the skills, and the honest answer to “so what can you actually do?”

title: 17  The Mini CEO’s Staff
text:
One agent became a department. A department gets staff.

New chapter — the management layer. Reviewer-agents auditing builder-agents, model choice and upgrade strategy (what to re-test when the model changes), cost as a first-class constraint, and the small print of accountability: the CEO signs, the staff drafts. Closes with the reader’s own staff charter written into their context folder.

title: 18  Conclusion: The Referee and the Department
text:
The tools will keep changing. The referee’s job will not.

What does not commoditise: the judgement that decides what to build, what “done” means, and what is worth shipping. The pipeline can be templated; the taste cannot. A closing tour of the reader’s portfolio — twelve repos, three documents each — and where the series goes next for readers who now want the layer underneath.
crumbs: 18  Conclusion: The Referee and the Department
